newsitem.title: ISRAEL: New Israeli Labour leader pays homage to Rabin.
newsitem.headline: New Israeli Labour leader pays homage to Rabin.

text.p: Former army chief Ehud Barak, the new leader of Israel's main opposition Labour party, pledged on Wednesday at the graveside of Yitzhak Rabin to continue the assassinated prime minister's struggle for peace.

"Yitzhak was my commander for decades, my mentor. I dare to say my friend in the last 30 years. He is the man who brought me into politics, into his government," said Barak, winner of Labour's leadership election on Tuesday.
"I see myself as following his legacy and trying to go in his footsteps. I feel highly committed to the struggle for peace," Barak said about Rabin, also a former army chief.
Rabin was assassinated in 1995 by a religious Jew opposed to his policy of trading occupied land for peace with the Arabs.

Barak, Israel's most decorated soldier, has said the Jewish state must take "calculated risks" for peace. He replaces former prime minister Shimon Peres who lost national elections a year ago to right-wing Likud party leader Benjamin Netanyahu.
In victory remarks Barak vowed to push for early elections to oust Prime Minister Netanyahu, whom he once commanded in an elite army unit.

"We'll do our best to make it a little bit earlier, maybe a year or two earlier," Barak told Reuters at Labour headquarters in Tel Aviv early on Wednesday. He later repeated his opposition to joining a national unity government with Netanyahu.

Israel's next general election is set for 2000 but Netanyahu's coalition, battered in its first year in power by crises in Middle East peacemaking and a corruption scandal, has only a slim majority in parliament, holding 66 of 120 seats.
Barak swept to a landslide victory over three other candidates, winning 51 percent of the vote. He is only the third Labour party leader since 1973.

Taking a page out of Netanyahu's post-election book, Barak made a morning-after pilgrimage to Jerusalem's Wailing Wall, Judaism's holiest site, but said in a radio interview before the visit he had no intention of offering any prayers.
About 15 ultranationalist Jews who gathered at the shrine to mark the 30th anniversary of Israel's capture of East Jerusalem heckled the new Labour leader.
"Shame on you," they shouted, getting within several metres of the closely guarded Barak.
The Labour contest was a milestone that marked a passing of the political torch from Peres, 73, and his predecessor Rabin.
"This is a first step towards hope, the first step towards renewal, the first step on the path to victory which will return us to the leadership of this country," Barak said.

Netanyahu edged out Peres in an upset election victory in 1996, in part by characterising the Nobel peace laureate as soft on security. Opinion polls have shown Barak neck and neck with Netanyahu, 47.

Barak beat out Yossi Beilin, an architect of Labour peace policies and Peres's protege, Shlomo Ben-Ami, a Moroccan-born novice politician with roots both in academia and among the disadvantaged, and Ephraim Sneh a former health minister.

Israeli media have portrayed Peres and Barak as at odds with each other but Peres told Reuters: "Undoubtedly he is an able man, he is an intelligent man, a man with experience and I do not see any reason why we can't work together."

At a news conference on Monday outlining his policy, Barak said Palestinians must have the right of self-determination which could lead to statehood on some of the land Israel captured in the 1967 Middle East war.

Barak joined Labour two years ago after shedding his uniform. Long before entering public life, Barak was a near-legendary military figure, widely reported to have participated in undercover killings of Arab guerrilla leaders.
Rabin's widow beamed at Labour party headquarters even as a tearful party activist, remembering her husband, embraced her.
"Besides respecting him and believing in his intellectual capacity, I voted for him because I see him as the winner and I want Labour to win, win, win," Leah Rabin told reporters.
